images.text:
Tour Guide: Welcome to our fantastic voyage through the Universe to learn more about our cosmic neighbors.
Vanessa: Louise, you really shouldn't use your cellphone on these tours. You'd better switch it off.
Louise: It might be my mother though. If I don't answer it, she'll get anxious. Hi, Mom, Yes. I've gotta go, I'm on a tour at the planetarium. Bye.
Vanessa: I bet she'll call you again in about an hour. Look at the constellations on the ceiling! Did you know there are 88 of them in total? Their names come from Latin and date back to Greek and Roman times.

Tour Guide: It can be difficult to recognize different constellations from a distance so we project the cosmos onto the dome above. Let me point out some interesting features like constellations, planets and ... if you look closely you will see an asteroid.
Louise: If I lean back any further I'll strain my neck. How do you know so much about them? What are they used for?
Vanessa: They may have been used by farmers to work out the seasons. It also could have been a way of telling which stars are which. I had to do some research on constellations at school. I remember I had to write a paragraph on a couple different ones.

Louise: It must have been interesting to learn about the stars. One of the constellations is Orion, right? Aren't the stars part of his belt? I could never find it.
Vanessa: Orion is one of the most prominent and recognizable constellations in the sky. If you can't locate this star, you'll need to spend a lot more time gazing into the night sky.
Louise: Well ... maybe I'll read your paragraph on Orion then, if you still have it.
Vanessa: That was ten years ago! If I still had that assignment in a box somewhere, it would be incredible!

Speculating About the Present
You often guess about situations based on what we know. You can choose modals based on how certain you are about your speculation.
Present
You use modal verbs in a situation when you need to explain a level of certainty in the present.

You use the structures:
must + infinitive
might / might not + infinitive
could / could not + infinitive
may / may not + infinitive
can't + infinitive

Examples:
I think I might need to call my mother back.
I must stop by the gift shop on our way out.

Will / won't
You use will and won't when we are very sure. This can be in the present, or in the future.

Example:
She'll be at home and thinking of me.
As soon as Ana confirms she's coming, I'll let you know.

Should / shouldn't
You use should and shouldn't to make assumptions about what is probably true.

Examples:
My mother should be home by now.
It shouldn't be too long now before the tour finishes.

Can
You use can for something that is generally possible.

Example:
Tourist areas can be expensive.
It might be my mother though.
It can be difficult to recognize different constellations from a distance.
Louise, the tour shouldn't take long.
I bet she'll call you again in about an hour.
Maybe I'll read your paragraph on Orion then, if you still have it?

When you want to speculate about the past, you use the modal + have + the past participle.

Example:
It must have been interesting to learn about the stars.
First Conditional
You use first conditional sentences to describe a real situation where the condition can happen.
You use first conditional sentences to talk about things which might happen in the future.

You use the form:
if + Present Simple, ... will + infinitive or modal with infinitive
If I don't answer it, she'll get anxious.
If I lean back any further, I'll strain my neck.
